title: Proving a greedy choice
objectives: Prove a greedy choice with an exchange argument.

screens.title: One room, six meetings
screens.prose: One meeting room and six requests. A meeting fills the room from its start time to its end time. Keep as many meetings as you can, with no two overlapping.
screens.question: Tap the meetings you keep.

Earliest finish: B (ends 5), D (ends 11), F (ends 14). 3 meetings.

Earliest start keeps A, which runs from 0 to 13 and blocks everything.
Step through the rules: they keep 2, 1 and 3 meetings.

The last rule keeps B, D and F.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the three counts.

screens.title: The exchange argument
screens.prose: Take any best schedule, OPT, sorted by time. Greedy's first meeting $g$ finishes earliest of all. Swap OPT's first meeting $o$ for $g$. This is an **exchange argument**: change a best answer into greedy's, one swap at a time, never making it worse.
screens.question: Why does the swapped schedule still have no overlap?

options.text: $g$ ends no later than $o$, so it leaves in time

options.why: Starting early does not help. What matters is that $g$ has left the room before the second meeting starts.
Length is not the point. A long $g$ from 0 to 5 would work just as well.

options.text: OPT's second meeting can move later
options.why: The swap leaves every other meeting where it is.

hints.text: What could $g$ clash with in the new schedule?
Only OPT's second meeting, which starts at 7.
$g$ ends at 5, no later than $o$'s 6, and the second meeting starts at 7.

feedback.correct: $g$ leaves the room no later than $o$ did.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which meeting $g$ could overlap.

byKey.starts: You compared start times. A clash with the second meeting depends on when $g$ ends.

explain.text: $g$ ends at 5, before $o$'s end at 6, so it cannot reach the meeting at 7. The count stays at 3 and nothing overlaps. Repeating the swap on the rest turns OPT into greedy's schedule, so greedy is optimal too.

Keep only the end of the last kept meeting.
For each `(s, e)` in end order: if `s >= end`, count it and set `end = e`.

widget.label: Rooms

hints.text: Slide the time and watch the count.
Look between 4 and 5.
At 4.5, A, B and C run together, and no moment has four. So 3 rooms.

feedback.correct: Three rooms: the peak number running at once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the moment with the most meetings running.

byKey.all: You opened a room per meeting. A room is free again once its meeting ends.
byKey.two: At time 4.5, A, B and C are all running, so two rooms are too few.

explain.text: The fewest rooms is the most meetings in progress at one moment, here 3 at time 4.5. Fewer rooms fail at that moment, and opening a room only when all are busy never needs more. A sweep over sorted start and end events finds the peak.

screens.title: Solve problem R
screens.prose: Write `min_rooms(intervals)`. Make an event `(s, 1)` for each start and `(e, -1)` for each end. Sort the events and track the peak of the running total. Sorting puts `(5, -1)` before `(5, 1)`, so a room freed at 5 serves a meeting starting at 5.

lines: n meetings (1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10⁵), each s e
(0 ≤ s < e ≤ 2·10⁹). A meeting may start
the moment another ends. Print the fewest
params.title: Problem R

screens.question: Write `min_rooms(intervals)`.

widget.solution:
def min_rooms(intervals):
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, 1))
        events.append((e, -1))
    events.sort()  # (5, -1) sorts before (5, 1)
    busy = best = 0
    for _, change in events:
        busy += change
        best = max(best, busy)
    return best
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: the six meetings, touching ends, identical and nested meetings, and four meetings that all overlap. Test 7 has 200,000 meetings.

hints.text: Two events per meeting, then one sort.
A running total of `+1` and `-1` is the number of busy rooms.
After sorting, add each change to `busy` and keep `best = max(best, busy)`. A min-heap of end times, as in `ds` lesson 17, also works.

feedback.correct: $2n$ events, one sort and one pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2's meetings touch at 3 and 5, so one room is enough. Process an end before a start at the same time.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has three identical meetings: they need 3 rooms.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has 200,000 meetings. Counting at every time point, or comparing every pair, is too slow.

explain.text: The events give an $O(n \log n)$ solution. The tie order, an end before a start, is problem M's touching rule. On the 200,000 random meetings the peak is 144 rooms.

screens.title: Greedy, then proof
screens.prose:
Problem M's greedy has the shape most greedies share:

```python
for x in sorted(items, key=KEY):
    if fits(x, chosen):
        chosen.append(x)
```

The whole problem is choosing `KEY`. The proof is an exchange: greedy's first choice can replace OPT's first without making it worse.
screens.question: Try the exchange on *earliest start*: swap OPT's first meeting, B, for A. What breaks?

options.text: A ends at 13 and overlaps D and F

options.why: Starting first says nothing about when A leaves the room. It runs until 13.

options.text: The number of meetings goes down
options.why: A swap replaces one meeting with one, so the count stays. The overlap is what breaks.

feedback.correct: The swap is safe only if greedy's choice ends no later.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare A's end with D's start.

explain.text: The swap is safe only when greedy's choice leaves the room no later than OPT's did. Earliest finish guarantees that; earliest start does not. When the exchange step fails, it points at the counterexample, here A.

screens.title: Auction slots
screens.prose: An exchange runs one call auction at a time. Eight client orders each need an auction over a fixed window, in minutes after 08:00. One may start the minute another ends. Fill as many orders as possible.
screens.question: How many orders can be filled?

hints.text: This is problem M.

Order 2 ends at 10, then 3 (10 to 25), 5 (25 to 40) and 8 (50 to 55).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort by end time and keep each window that fits.

byKey.start: 3 is what earliest start gives: order 1, from 0 to 30, blocks four others.
byKey.all: Several windows overlap, so one auction at a time cannot fill all eight.

explain.text: Earliest finish fills 4 orders: 2, 3, 5 and 8. In an interview, give the reason in one sentence: any best schedule can swap in the earliest-finishing order. That sentence is what the interviewer marks.

ideas: A greedy sorts by one key and keeps what fits; the whole difficulty is choosing the key.
An exchange argument proves the key: greedy's first choice can replace a best answer's first without making it worse.
A greedy that passes the samples is still a guess until it has a proof or a stress test.

formula.name: Earliest finish
formula.tex: \text{keep } (s, e) \text{ in order of } e \text{ whenever } s \ge \text{last kept end}
formula.note: Use `s > end` instead when touching meetings clash.
